newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Commerzbank CEO wants level playing field.
newsitem.headline: Commerzbank CEO wants level playing field.

text.p: Martin Kohlhaussen, chief executive of Commerzbank AG, said the European Commission in Brussels would hopefully soon decide in a dispute between Germany's private banks and Bonn over a plan by the German government to protect publicly-owned banks.
Kohlhaussen told a briefing at the International Monetary Conference (IMF) that all Germany's private banks wanted was a level playing field and hopefully Brussel would soon make a decision.
He said there was a "struggle" going on between private German banks and the so-called Landesbanken, banks owned by regional or local governments in Germany.
The struggle was particularly with Westdeutsche Landesbank (WestLB) and revolved around the issue of whether equity that has been given to them has been properly paid for.
"Return on equity which is the basis for their expansion is not paid the same way that we have to pay on equity," Kohlhaussen said.

The dispute centres on a complaint filed in 1994 by the Federal Association of German Banks, which represents private sector banks, that 11 billion marks of state capital transferred to publicly-owned regional banks since 1990 constituted a breach of EU subsidy rules.
The German upper house recently proposed that Landesbanken should be exempt from European Union (EU) competition laws in a new community treaty, known as Maastricht 2.

Landesbanken are owned by their respective federal states and savings bank associations. They do not offer retail banking but compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing. State guarantees available to the Landesbanken have enabled some of them to gain top credit ratings.
